title: Numbers, age, and phone numbers
goal: Count to twenty, say your age, read out phone numbers, and use کتنا / کتنی / کتنے correctly.
bekal: ask and give someone's age in the right form
say and write a Pakistani phone number

dialogs.title: مکالمہ — زبان کے اسکول میں
dialogs.intro: Budi is signing up for an Urdu course. The receptionist fills in the form as she asks him questions.

lines.speaker: کلرک:
lines.text: السلام علیکم۔ آپ کا پورا نام کیا ہے؟
lines.baca: as-salāmu alaikum. āp kā pūrā nām kyā hai?
lines.id: Peace be upon you. What's your full name?
lines.literal: peace upon you. you of full name what is?

lines.speaker: بودی:
lines.text: بودی سنتوسو۔ میں انڈونیشیا سے ہوں۔

lines.text: اچھا۔ کلاس کتنے گھنٹے کی ہے؟
lines.baca: achchhā. klās kitne ghanṭe kī hai?

notes: **Age is expressed with a possessive, not with "to be … old".** The question آپ کی عمر کتنی ہے؟ literally means "your age how much is?". Notice کی and کتنی — both are feminine because **عمر is feminine**. A shorter form that's also correct and more casual: آپ کتنے سال کے ہیں؟

**After a number, the noun often stays singular.** For example چوبیس سال, not چوبیس سالیں. With units of time, money, and measurement, Urdu uses the singular after a number — a bit like English "a twenty-four-year-old" or "a ten-dollar bill". But with countable things, the plural is used: آٹھ لڑکیاں and چار لڑکے.

**The word کتنا changes three ways.** کتنا پانی؟ (water, masculine) · کتنی چائے؟ (tea, feminine) · کتنے لوگ؟ (people, masculine plural). It ends in ـا, so it belongs to the adjectives that change — the rule from unit 2 applies exactly.

**Phone numbers are read digit by digit.** Pakistanis read 0312 as صفر، تین، ایک، دو, not as "three hundred twelve". Zero is صفر (*sifar*) — the word that traveled through Arabic to become "cipher" and "zero" in European languages, and the concept itself came from India. Pakistani mobile numbers always start with 03.

**The word معلوم is Urdu's way of saying "know".** The question معلوم ہے؟ = "do you know?", literally "is it known?". The full forms: مجھے معلوم ہے ("I know") and مجھے نہیں معلوم ("I don't know"). Notice the subject is مجھے, not میں — this is a dative sentence, and unit 10 is all about the pattern.

**The word اچھا works like English "OK".** Besides meaning "good", it's used on its own to show you're listening and accept what was said: اچھا۔ With a rising tone, اچھا؟ means "oh really?" or "is that so?". It's the word you'll say most after جی.

grammars.title: Numbers 1 to 20
body: There's no shortcut: Urdu has a separate word for every number up to a hundred, and the first twenty need to be in your head so firmly that they come out without thinking. Learn them in groups of five, out loud, counting on your fingers.
after: Two things help you remember. **First**, the word دو sounds like "two" and they really are related — both come from the same Indo-European word, as do تین and "three". **Second**, the numbers 11–18 all end in **ـرہ / ـہ**, a worn-down form of دس (ten), while 19 is already reaching for 20: انیس literally means "one less than twenty". That "one less" pattern repeats at 29, 39, 49, and so on — see the numbers page at the back of the book.
Zero is صفر (*sifar*), and half is آدھا (*ādhā*).

grammars.title: Asking about amounts and prices
body: The sentences below cover almost every number question you'll ask in your first weeks. Learn them as whole sentences, not as formulas.
after: ⚠️ Notice that prices are asked with **کتنے کا**, not کتنا. Literally it means "of how many" — the item is "worth" so many rupees. What decides کا or کی is **the item asked about**, not the money: یہ قمیض کتنے کی ہے؟ because قمیض is feminine.

blocks.title: Ordinal numbers, and three irregular ones
items: The ordinals "first, second, third" in Urdu are پہلا، دوسرا، تیسرا, and all three are **impossible to guess** from ایک، دو، تین — much like English *first* and *second*. From the fourth on, the pattern is regular: number + ـواں — چوتھا (fourth, still a bit special), پانچواں، چھٹا، ساتواں، آٹھواں، نواں، دسواں.
They all end in ـا, so they all change: پہلا دن (the first day), پہلی کتاب (the first book), پہلے دن (on the first day).

The word دوسرا does two jobs: "second" and also "other". The phrase دوسرا آدمی can mean "the second man" or "another man", depending on context. If you want to say "another" clearly, use **اور ایک** or **کوئی اور**.

exercises.prompt: Write these numbers as Urdu words.
Choose the right form: کتنا، کتنی، or کتنے.

items: There are twelve students in the class.
The class is two hours long.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in the right order.
items: ہیں / بارہ / کلاس / طالب علم / میں

answers: میری عمر بیس سال ہے۔ — کلاس میں بارہ طالب علم ہیں۔ — آپ کا فون نمبر کیا ہے؟ — کلاس دو گھنٹے کی ہے۔ — مجھے نہیں معلوم۔
آپ کی عمر کتنی ہے؟ — میری عمر بیس سال ہے۔ — کلاس میں بارہ طالب علم ہیں۔ — کلاس دو گھنٹے کی ہے۔ — مجھے معلوم نہیں ہے۔
wave: Count backward from بیس to ایک out loud before bed, three nights in a row. After that, you won't need to think about the numbers anymore.
